The attack failed on the wording, which was the only place this line could have broken, because it is English-original and there is no translator to drift. I fetched the Penelope (University of Chicago) reading text of Hydriotaphia chapter V myself rather than trusting the verifier's summary of it, and the sentence comes back character for character: 'Life is a pure flame, and we live by an invisible Sun within us.' The capital S on Sun is the edition's, so the card will print what the page prints. THE SURROUNDING TEXT CONFIRMS THE PLACE. The verifier said the line sits immediately before the sentence beginning 'A small fire sufficeth for life'; the fetch returns exactly that continuation, and it continues in Browne's own 1658 spelling ('wisedom of funerall Laws', 'prodigall blazes', 'an Urne'), which is the tell that this is a Browne text and not a modernised anthology squib. That matters here: the quoted sentence happens to contain no archaic spelling of its own, so a modernising editor would have left it identical, and the archaic spelling two clauses later is what proves the surrounding text was not silently cleaned up. Chapter V is correct.

WHAT I TRIED AND COULD NOT MAKE STICK. (1) Anthology truncation. 'We live by an invisible sun within us' circulates on its own as a decontextualised uplift fragment, lower-cased, and I expected the proposal to be that fragment dressed back up. It is not: the proposal carries the whole sentence with its first clause, in the printed capitalisation. (2) Misattribution. Browne is not on the brief's trap list and this is not one of the roving orphan lines; it is an anchor sentence of a canonical work. (3) Speaker. There is none to name: Hydriotaphia is Browne in his own voice, a discourse, not a fiction with characters, so no parenthetical speaker is owed. (4) Scope. First published 1658, not scripture despite the resurrection matter running alongside it in chapter V, not film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory.

EVERY OTHER GATE. shipped.js on the exact line with 'Thomas Browne': shipped [], near [], thomas browne at 0 of 3 for the year, cap 3, not banned; he is not on personsAtCap and not in personsUsed at all, so he costs the month nothing and adds a seventeenth-century voice the year is short of. Source line 'Thomas Browne, Hydriotaphia, Urn-Burial, chapter V (1658)' is 56 characters, leads with the author's name, gives work then locator then date, carries no dash of any kind, and needs no translator parenthesis. Quotation ends in a full stop; no straight double quote and no quote mark at all in it; prose kept as prose. Tag Essay is the right one of the seven: Hydriotaphia is a discourse, and of Philosophy, Poetry, Drama, Fiction, Essay, Correspondence and Diary, Essay is the form of the work. Publishable: chapter V is the famous meditation on burial and it does carry ash and urns nearby, but the sentence taken is the opposite of graphic, it is the flame-and-sun image, and nothing in it needs a warning.

THEME AND THE SIX A.M. TEST. August is impermanence, and the blurb splits it into the poets on passing and the philosophers on what stays. This is squarely the second half: a pure flame is the most impermanent thing there is, and Browne's move is to locate it in an invisible Sun that does not go out. Famous-and-bleak is the failure mode the rule warns about, and a reader could fairly say chapter V as a whole is bleak. This sentence is not: it is the warm one, and it is the sentence the chapter is known by. It is the strongest of the four lines I was given.

ONE SMALL NOTE FOR THE EDITOR, WHICH IS NOT A REFUTATION. The note field is empty. That is allowed, but this is a line whose author most readers meet as 'Sir Thomas Browne', and a one-clause note placing him (a physician writing on burial urns dug up in Norfolk) would earn its space. The byline itself is right as it stands: rule 5 asks for the author's name, not his title.
